Can a 10-euro sensor replace a 100,000-euro analyser? Calibrating low-cost air quality sensors¶

A multi-sensor device sat for a year (March 2004 to April 2005) at road level in an Italian city, next to a certified reference analyser. Every hour it recorded the response of five cheap metal-oxide sensors plus temperature and humidity, and the analyser recorded the true concentrations of carbon monoxide, benzene and nitrogen dioxide. The question every city with a sensor network asks: can the cheap sensors be calibrated to read like the analyser, and how long does the calibration last?

The notebook covers the unglamorous parts that decide the answer:

  • Missing data coded as -200, with large gaps, and how it should be handled;
  • Cross-sensitivity: cheap sensors respond to temperature and humidity as well as to the gas;
  • Drift: a model fitted in the first months is tested on the last months, six months later;
  • Re-calibration: how much of the lost accuracy comes back when the model is refitted every week on the most recent reference readings.

Data: Air Quality from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (De Vito et al., 2008; CC BY 4.0). The notebook downloads it (about 1.5 MB) into AIR_DIR on the first run.

In [1]:
import os
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

DATA_DIR = Path(os.environ.get("AIR_DIR", "air_data"))
DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
AMBER, BLUE, GREY = "#e8a33d", "#2b6cb0", "#a0aec0"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.25, "figure.dpi": 110})

1. Load the data and look at what is missing¶

The file uses semicolons, decimal commas and the value -200 for "no reading". If that were left in, a linear model would treat -200 as a real concentration. It is converted to a proper missing value first.

In [2]:
zip_path = DATA_DIR / "air_quality.zip"
if not zip_path.exists():
    urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/360/air+quality.zip", zip_path)
with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_path) as z:
    raw = pd.read_csv(z.open("AirQualityUCI.csv"), sep=";", decimal=",")
raw = raw.loc[:, ~raw.columns.str.startswith("Unnamed")].dropna(how="all")
raw["time"] = pd.to_datetime(raw.Date + " " + raw.Time.str.replace(".", ":", regex=False), format="%d/%m/%Y %H:%M:%S")
air = raw.drop(columns=["Date", "Time"]).set_index("time").replace(-200, np.nan)
air = air.rename(columns={"CO(GT)": "CO", "C6H6(GT)": "benzene", "NO2(GT)": "NO2", "NOx(GT)": "NOx", "NMHC(GT)": "NMHC",
                          "PT08.S1(CO)": "S1_CO", "PT08.S2(NMHC)": "S2_NMHC", "PT08.S3(NOx)": "S3_NOx", "PT08.S4(NO2)": "S4_NO2", "PT08.S5(O3)": "S5_O3"})

REFERENCE = ["CO", "benzene", "NO2", "NOx", "NMHC"]               # the analyser (ground truth)
SENSORS = ["S1_CO", "S2_NMHC", "S3_NOx", "S4_NO2", "S5_O3"]        # the cheap sensors
WEATHER = ["T", "RH", "AH"]
print(f"{len(air):,} hourly records, {air.index.min():%d %b %Y} to {air.index.max():%d %b %Y}")
(air.isna().mean() * 100).round(1).to_frame("% missing").T

monthly_missing = air.isna().groupby([air.index.year, air.index.month]).mean() * 100
monthly_missing.index = [f"{y}-{m:02d}" for y, m in monthly_missing.index]
cols = REFERENCE + SENSORS + WEATHER
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.5]})
share = air[cols].isna().mean() * 100
axes[0].barh(cols[::-1], share[cols][::-1], color=[AMBER if c in REFERENCE else BLUE if c in SENSORS else GREY for c in cols[::-1]])
axes[0].set_xlabel("% of hours with no reading")
axes[0].set_title("Reference gas analysers (amber) miss far more than sensors", fontsize=9)
im = axes[1].imshow(monthly_missing[cols].T.values, cmap="Oranges", aspect="auto", vmin=0, vmax=100)
axes[1].set_yticks(range(len(cols)), cols, fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(len(monthly_missing)), monthly_missing.index, rotation=70, fontsize=8)
axes[1].grid(False)
axes[1].set_title("Share missing by month", fontsize=9)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.8, label="%")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The sensors are missing together (3.9% of hours, when the whole device was off) while the reference analysers go missing more often (about 18%, probably during calibration and maintenance). The NMHC analyser is missing 90% of the time and is dropped as a target. For every question below, hours without a reading of the target cannot be scored and are removed, as are hours when the sensor device itself was off.

Every cheap sensor is strongly tied to the gases (the CO sensor S1_CO correlates 0.88 with carbon monoxide), but they also correlate with each other because they all follow the same traffic. That is helpful (a sensor for one gas carries information about another) and a trap (a model can lean on the wrong sensor). Note also that benzene correlates 0.98 with the NMHC sensor, so tightly that it looks like an almost direct function of that sensor. That makes it an easy target, so carbon monoxide is the main one here.

3. Calibration over time: train early, test late¶

Real deployments are judged on the future, so the data is split by time: the first six months to fit (March to August 2004), September and October to choose settings, and November 2004 to April 2005 as the test, from half a year to a year after the first measurement. Any sensor drift or seasonal change shows up in the test.

In [6]:
FEATURES = SENSORS + WEATHER
clean = air.dropna(subset=FEATURES).copy()
clean["dow"] = clean.index.dayofweek

def split(target):
    d = clean.dropna(subset=[target])
    return (d[d.index < "2004-09-01"], d[(d.index >= "2004-09-01") & (d.index < "2004-11-01")], d[d.index >= "2004-11-01"])

train, valid, test = split("CO")
print(f"carbon monoxide: train {len(train):,} h | validation {len(valid):,} h | test {len(test):,} h")
pd.DataFrame({"train (Mar-Aug 2004)": train.CO.describe(), "test (Nov 2004-Apr 2005)": test.CO.describe()}).T.round(2)

carbon monoxide: train 3,145 h | validation 947 h | test 3,252 h

The four models for each gas:

  • One sensor, linear: the textbook calibration of the matching sensor (for CO the S1_CO sensor).
  • All sensors + weather, linear: uses the other sensors and the temperature and humidity to correct the reading.
  • Gradient-boosted trees: lets the relationship be non-linear. Two settings are tried on the validation months.
  • Weekly re-calibration (linear): every week the linear model is refitted on the previous 8 weeks of reference readings, as if a technician compared the device with the analyser regularly. This is the only model that sees recent ground truth.
In [7]:
MATCHING = {"CO": "S1_CO", "benzene": "S2_NMHC", "NO2": "S4_NO2", "NOx": "S3_NOx"}

def rolling_predict(frame, target, start, weeks_back=8):
    """Refit a linear model every week on the previous `weeks_back` weeks of reference data, then predict the coming week."""
    preds = pd.Series(np.nan, index=frame.index)
    fallback = LinearRegression().fit(frame[frame.index < start][FEATURES], frame[frame.index < start][target])
    for w0 in pd.date_range(start, frame.index.max() + pd.Timedelta(days=7), freq="7D"):
        cur = frame[(frame.index >= w0) & (frame.index < w0 + pd.Timedelta(days=7))]
        if cur.empty:
            continue
        hist = frame[(frame.index >= w0 - pd.Timedelta(weeks=weeks_back)) & (frame.index < w0)]
        model = LinearRegression().fit(hist[FEATURES], hist[target]) if len(hist) >= 100 else fallback
        preds.loc[cur.index] = model.predict(cur[FEATURES])
    return preds[preds.index >= start]

def run(target):
    tr, va, te = split(target)
    out = {}
    out["One sensor, linear"] = LinearRegression().fit(tr[[MATCHING[target]]], tr[target]).predict(te[[MATCHING[target]]])
    out["All sensors + weather, linear"] = LinearRegression().fit(tr[FEATURES], tr[target]).predict(te[FEATURES])
    grid = []
    for lr in [0.05, 0.1]:
        for leaves in [8, 16]:
            m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=lr, max_leaf_nodes=leaves, max_iter=300, random_state=0).fit(tr[FEATURES], tr[target])
            grid.append((mean_absolute_error(va[target], m.predict(va[FEATURES])), lr, leaves))
    _, lr, leaves = min(grid)
    trva = pd.concat([tr, va])
    out["Gradient-boosted trees"] = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=lr, max_leaf_nodes=leaves, max_iter=300, random_state=0).fit(
        trva[FEATURES], trva[target]).predict(te[FEATURES])
    out["Weekly re-calibration (linear)"] = rolling_predict(pd.concat([tr, va, te]), target, pd.Timestamp("2004-11-01")).reindex(te.index).to_numpy()
    return te, out

def score(truth, pred):
    return {"RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((truth - pred) ** 2))), "MAE": mean_absolute_error(truth, pred), "R2": r2_score(truth, pred),
            "bias": float(np.mean(pred - truth))}

test_co, preds_co = run("CO")
results_co = pd.DataFrame({name: score(test_co.CO.to_numpy(), p) for name, p in preds_co.items()}).T
results_co.round(3)
Out[7]:

Gradient-boosted trees 0.609 0.399 0.849 -0.095

4. Drift: how fast does a calibration go stale?¶

The error of the static models (fitted once, in 2004) against the weekly re-calibrated one, month by month through the test period. If the sensors or the environment change, the static error and the bias should grow.

In [9]:
static_linear, static_trees, recal = preds_co["All sensors + weather, linear"], preds_co["Gradient-boosted trees"], preds_co["Weekly re-calibration (linear)"]
frame = pd.DataFrame({"truth": test_co.CO.to_numpy(), "static linear": static_linear, "static trees": static_trees, "re-calibrated": recal}, index=test_co.index)
monthly = frame.groupby(frame.index.to_period("M"))
rmse_by_month = pd.DataFrame({c: monthly.apply(lambda g: np.sqrt(np.mean((g[c] - g.truth) ** 2))) for c in ["static linear", "static trees", "re-calibrated"]})
bias_by_month = pd.DataFrame({c: monthly.apply(lambda g: np.mean(g[c] - g.truth)) for c in ["static linear", "static trees", "re-calibrated"]})
months = [str(m) for m in rmse_by_month.index]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4))
for col, color in zip(rmse_by_month.columns, [BLUE, "#38a169", AMBER]):
    axes[0].plot(months, rmse_by_month[col], marker="o", color=color, label=col, lw=2)
    axes[1].plot(months, bias_by_month[col], marker="o", color=color, label=col, lw=2)
axes[0].set_ylabel("RMSE (mg/m3)")
axes[0].set_title("Error by month", fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="#4a5568", lw=1)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Average error: prediction minus truth (mg/m3)")
axes[1].set_title("Bias by month (below 0 = reads too low)", fontsize=10)
for ax in axes:
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45, labelsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
rmse_by_month.round(2).T

5. Which gases can be calibrated best?¶

The same four models for benzene, nitrogen dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Gases whose sensors respond less specifically, or whose analyser data is noisier, are harder.

In [11]:
rows = {}
for target in ["CO", "benzene", "NO2", "NOx"]:
    te, preds = run(target)
    for name, p in preds.items():
        rows[(target, name)] = score(te[target].to_numpy(), p)
all_gases = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
all_gases.index.names = ["gas", "model"]
r2_table = all_gases.R2.unstack("model")[["One sensor, linear", "All sensors + weather, linear", "Gradient-boosted trees", "Weekly re-calibration (linear)"]]
r2_table.round(3)

6. What does the best static model rely on?¶

Permutation importance: shuffle one input at a time on the test months and see how much the error grows.

In [12]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

tr, va, te = split("CO")
trva = pd.concat([tr, va])
forest = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=0.05, max_leaf_nodes=8, max_iter=300, random_state=0).fit(trva[FEATURES], trva.CO)
imp = permutation_importance(forest, te[FEATURES], te.CO, n_repeats=5, random_state=0, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
importance = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=FEATURES).sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.9))
ax.barh(importance.index, importance.values, color=[BLUE if f in SENSORS else AMBER for f in importance.index])
ax.set_xlabel("Increase in mean absolute error when the input is shuffled (mg/m3)")
ax.set_title("Inputs the CO model relies on (blue = sensors, amber = weather)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(3).to_frame("extra error")

What the results say¶

  • The ground truth is patchy. The sensors are off in 3.9% of the hours, but the reference analysers are missing much more: carbon monoxide 18.0%, nitrogen dioxide and oxides 17.5%, and NMHC 90.2% (that analyser stops working after about April 2004), with up to roughly half of the hours missing for CO and NO2 in October 2004. The -200 placeholder in the file would have been silently treated as a reading by a naive model.
  • The air has a traffic rhythm. On working days carbon monoxide peaks at about 3.5 mg/m3 around 8-9 a.m. and about 4.2 in the evening rush, while weekends have no morning peak (about 1.7 at midday). The monthly average is highest in October to December (about 2.7) and lowest in August (1.3, when the city is probably emptier, an interpretation) and in the partial month of April 2005.
  • Calibrating for the future is harder than the textbook suggests. The test months (November 2004 to April 2005) have higher carbon monoxide than the training months (average 2.25 against 1.92 mg/m3, maximum 11.9 against 8.1). The standard calibration, a straight line from the matching CO sensor, gets an R2 of 0.72 and an RMSE of 0.84 mg/m3. Adding the other sensors and the weather made the linear model worse (R2 0.70, and it reads 0.61 mg/m3 too low on average): relationships learned in the summer do not hold in the winter, so more inputs mean more ways to be wrong.
  • A non-linear model does better, and so does regular re-calibration. Gradient-boosted trees reach an R2 of 0.85 (RMSE 0.61) and weekly re-calibration of the linear model on the previous eight weeks of reference readings gets 0.83 (RMSE 0.65) with almost no bias (-0.02). The static linear model is too low in every single test month (by 0.47 to 0.78 mg/m3), whereas re-calibration keeps the average error close to zero.
  • The CO model hardly uses the CO sensor. Shuffling the NMHC sensor raises the model's error by 0.98 mg/m3, against 0.11 for the sensor that is supposed to measure CO, and 0.03 or less for the rest. The cheap sensors respond to traffic in general, and the best-behaved one carries most of the information, which is cross-sensitivity working in the analyst's favour but not something a datasheet would promise.
  • Some gases calibrate easily and others do not. Benzene is easy (test R2 of 0.96 for the single sensor and 0.995 for the trees), partly because it follows the NMHC sensor so closely. Nitrogen dioxide breaks static calibration: the single-sensor line gets an R2 of -2.35, the trees -0.18 and the multi-sensor line 0.50, and only weekly re-calibration recovers a usable 0.62. For nitrogen oxides re-calibration is the clear winner (R2 0.87 against 0.68 for the trees and -0.43 for the static line).
  • The practical lesson. A cheap sensor is not a fixed instrument. For the gases it tracks well it can be calibrated once and used for months, but for the ones it tracks badly a regular comparison with a reference analyser is worth more than a smarter model.

Limits: one device at one roadside location over one year, so conclusions about drift and seasons rest on a single deployment; hours without a reference reading (18% for CO) are removed and may not be missing at random; the weekly re-calibration assumes that reference readings of the previous eight weeks are available, which a real network may not have; the test period is both later and different in season, so drift and seasonality are mixed together; R2 is reported without confidence intervals.

Techniques covered: cleaning a missing-value code, time-based train, validation and test split, linear regression and gradient boosting, a rolling re-calibration loop, error and bias by month, permutation importance and a comparison across four target gases.
